records.title: 4T65-E Transmission Failure and Hard Shifts
records.description: The 4T65-E automatic transmission used in the 2000-2013 Impala is one of the most failure-prone GM transmissions. Common failures include the 1-2 accumulator piston cracking (causing harsh 1-2 shift), pressure control solenoid failure (erratic shifts and slipping), and the forward clutch hub cracking (complete loss of forward gears). The 3.8L supercharged models are especially hard on the 4T65-E due to higher torque output. Many 4T65-E transmissions fail between 80,000-120,000 miles.
records.solution: For early-stage issues (harsh shifts, slipping), a fluid change with ACDelco DEXRON VI and a pressure control solenoid replacement ($200-$400) may resolve the problem. Once the transmission is slipping badly or has lost a gear, a rebuild ($2,000-$3,000) or remanufactured transmission ($2,500-$3,500 installed) is required. When rebuilding, upgrade the 1-2 accumulator piston to the updated design and install a TransGo shift kit ($50) for improved durability. Change fluid every 30,000 miles to maximize the life of this transmission.
symptoms: Harsh or banging 1-2 shift
Transmission slipping under acceleration
Loss of 3rd or 4th gear
Delayed engagement when shifting to Drive
Check engine light with transmission codes
Burnt fluid smell from dipstick

communityRecommendations.content: Change the 4T65-E fluid every 30,000 miles with DEXRON VI — not "lifetime fill." GM stopped calling it lifetime fill because these transmissions were failing in droves. A $150 fluid change is cheap insurance against a $3,000 rebuild.

records.title: Erratic Fuel Gauge from Faulty Fuel Level Sensor / Sending Unit
records.description: The in-tank fuel level sensor (part of the sending unit on the fuel pump module) is a common failure on the Impala. The sensor's small metal contact 'teeth' wear against the resistor card as the float arm moves, and the arm itself can stick or bind. The result is a gauge that reads inaccurately or swings erratically between full and empty, often unrelated to actual fuel level. This can leave owners stranded by a gauge that shows fuel remaining when the tank is near empty.
records.solution: Distinguish sender vs. gauge: an erratic/fluctuating needle points to the fuel level sensor/sending unit, while a gauge that won't rest at E (key off) or reach F (full tank) points to the gauge/cluster. On many Impalas the sender is reachable through an access cover in the trunk floor without dropping the tank. Replace the fuel level sensor or the complete fuel pump/sender module. A GM-approved fuel system cleaner can help if deposits on the sender are the cause.
symptoms: Fuel gauge fluctuates between full and empty
Gauge stuck on full or empty
Reading doesn't match actual fuel level
Low-fuel light behaves erratically
Gauge jumps when turning or braking

records.title: Front ABS Wheel Speed Sensor Wiring Harness Failure (C0035)
records.description: The 2006-2013 Impala is notorious for internal breaks in the front ABS wheel-speed-sensor wiring harness. The factory routes and clamps the harness such that steering movement repeatedly flexes the wire; the copper conductors fracture inside the insulation while the outer jacket looks perfectly intact, making it hard to spot. The result is intermittent ABS, traction control, and StabiliTrak warnings — often appearing or clearing when the wheel is turned. Left front (C0035) is the most common, but both sides fail.
records.solution: Confirm with a continuity/wiggle test from the EBCM connector to the wheel-speed sensor while flexing the harness at the wheel — the break is usually near where the harness is clamped. GM offers side-specific and year-specific repair pigtails to splice in rather than replacing the entire harness; aftermarket replacement harnesses (e.g., for 2006-2013 Impala) are also available. Repair or replace the affected front harness/pigtail.
symptoms: Intermittent ABS, Traction Control, and StabiliTrak warning lights
Warnings appear/clear when turning the steering wheel
Speedometer or ABS dropout at low speed
No visible damage to wire insulation

records.title: HVAC Blend Door Actuator Clicking and Uneven Cabin Temperature
records.description: A repetitive clicking or knocking sound from behind the dash — often constant, sometimes only when the car is running or turned off — is a classic Impala blend door actuator failure. The plastic gears inside the small actuator motor strip out, so the actuator can no longer position the blend door. On dual-zone systems there are separate left and right actuators; a stuck door means one side blows hot while the other blows cold, or the temperature won't respond to the setting.
records.solution: Locate the clicking actuator (temperature/blend, mode, or recirc — the Dorman 604-108 covers common Impala blend-door applications). Replace the failed actuator; pulling its fuse only silences the clicking temporarily and is not a fix. Many Impala actuators self-calibrate on install: set temperature to full hot or cold, reconnect the battery, cycle the key on, and let the motors auto-calibrate.
symptoms: Repetitive clicking/knocking behind the dash
One side blows hot, the other cold (dual-zone)
Temperature doesn't change with setting
Air comes from wrong vents
Clicking continues after engine off

records.title: Ignition Switch Failure and Recall (NHTSA 14V-394)
records.description: The 2003-2006 Impala was included in the massive GM ignition switch recall affecting millions of vehicles. The ignition switch has a weak detent spring that allows the key to slip from the "Run" position to the "Accessory" or "Off" position while driving. When this happens, the engine shuts off, the power steering and brake boost are lost, and the airbags are disabled — all without warning. The issue is exacerbated by heavy key chains that add weight and leverage on the ignition cylinder. This defect was linked to numerous fatalities.
records.solution: Check the NHTSA recall database (NHTSA.gov) with your VIN — this is recall 14V-394 and the repair is FREE at any GM dealer regardless of mileage or ownership history. The dealer replaces the ignition switch assembly with an updated design that has a stronger detent spring. Until the recall is completed, remove all extra keys and accessories from your key chain — use only the vehicle key with nothing else attached. NEVER ignore this recall; it is a critical safety issue.
symptoms: Engine shuts off unexpectedly while driving
Key turns to accessory position on its own
Airbag warning light illuminated
Power steering lost suddenly
Dashboard goes dark momentarily while driving
Stalling when hitting bumps or turning

communityRecommendations.content: This recall is FREE at any GM dealer forever — there is no time or mileage limit. Check NHTSA.gov with your VIN immediately. This defect has caused fatalities. Do not drive the car with extra weight on the key chain.

records.title: Instrument Cluster Stepper Motor Gauge Failure
records.description: These Impala gauge clusters use small stepper motors to drive each needle, and GM's era-wide stepper-motor defect makes them fail prematurely. Typically one gauge sticks or reads wildly wrong first (speedometer stuck at 60 while parked, fuel pegged on full, temperature slammed to the red on a cold engine, or a stuck tachometer), then others follow over time. It starts intermittent and progressively worsens, and can be a safety concern when the speedometer is inaccurate.
records.solution: The most recommended fix is to send the original cluster to a specialty repair shop that replaces the failed stepper motors (and burnt bulbs) — because it's your original unit, the mileage and VIN stay correct and no reprogramming is needed on reinstall. Alternatively, install a replacement/rebuilt cluster, which then requires programming to the vehicle's VIN and mileage. DIY stepper-motor kits (e.g., X27.168 motors) exist for the experienced.
symptoms: Speedometer reads wrong / stuck while parked
Fuel or temperature gauge stuck or pegged
Tachometer stuck or erratic
Needles sweep or drop to zero randomly
One gauge fails, then others follow

records.title: Intake Manifold Gasket Leak (3.4L/3.8L V6)
records.description: The 3.4L and 3.8L V6 engines in 2000-2005 Impalas use Dex-Cool compatible intake manifold gaskets that deteriorate over time, causing coolant to leak externally or internally into the oil. External leaks appear as dried orange coolant trails on the engine block. Internal leaks contaminate the engine oil with coolant, turning it into a milky sludge that can destroy the engine bearings. This was one of the most widespread GM engine problems of the era and led to multiple class-action lawsuits.
records.solution: Replace both intake manifold gaskets with the updated Fel-Pro design (not the original GM plastic gaskets). Parts cost $30-$80 for a quality gasket set. Labor is 4-6 hours ($400-$700) due to the need to remove the upper and lower intake manifolds, fuel rail, and wiring. If coolant has mixed with oil (milky dipstick), perform multiple oil changes in rapid succession to flush the contamination. Check the oil frequently after repair to ensure no internal damage occurred.
symptoms: Orange/pink coolant leaking on engine block
Milky or chocolate-milk colored oil on dipstick
Coolant level dropping with no visible external leak
White smoke from exhaust
Overheating at idle
Sweet coolant smell from engine bay

communityRecommendations.content: If your oil looks milky or foamy on the dipstick, STOP DRIVING immediately. Coolant-contaminated oil will destroy the engine bearings within a few hundred miles. Tow the car to a shop.

Use Fel-Pro updated intake manifold gaskets — NOT the original GM plastic design. The Fel-Pro gaskets use a metal carrier with improved sealing material that does not deteriorate with Dex-Cool coolant.

records.title: Steering Intermediate Shaft Clunk
records.description: The intermediate steering shaft on the 2006-2020 Impala develops a clunk or pop felt through the steering wheel when turning, especially at low speeds and when going over bumps. The intermediate shaft connects the steering column to the steering gear and uses a slip joint that loses its lubrication over time, causing a binding and releasing action that creates the clunk. The noise is most noticeable when turning while going over speed bumps or entering driveways. GM issued TSB 08-02-32-007 for this issue.
records.solution: The intermediate shaft can be temporarily improved by injecting lithium grease into the slip joint through a small hole drilled in the shaft boot. The permanent fix is replacement of the intermediate steering shaft with the updated GM design ($150-$300 for parts, $100-$200 labor). The updated shaft has improved lubrication retention. Some owners apply grease every 6-12 months as a cheaper maintenance approach rather than full replacement.
symptoms: Clunk or pop felt in steering wheel when turning
Noise when turning over bumps or uneven surfaces
Steering feels notchy or catches during turns
Clunk most noticeable at low speeds
Pop when going from left to right turn

citations.title: YouTube Repair Video by ChrisFix on Fixing Steering Intermediate Shaft Clunk on Chevrolet Impala

communityRecommendations.content: Before paying for a new intermediate shaft, try injecting white lithium grease into the slip joint. Pull back the rubber boot, inject grease, and work the shaft back and forth. This fixes the clunk for 6-12 months and costs $5.

records.title: Passlock Security System No-Start Condition
records.description: The Passlock anti-theft system causes intermittent no-start conditions where the security light flashes and the fuel pump is disabled. The ignition lock cylinder contains a Hall-effect sensor that reads a resistance value; when contacts wear or corrode, the BCM detects a mismatch and locks out fuel delivery. The problem typically worsens progressively from occasional to daily. 225+ complaints were filed for the 2002 model year alone.
symptoms: Security/theft light flashing on dashboard
Engine cranks but will not start
No-start condition occurs more frequently over time
Car starts after waiting 10+ minutes

records.title: Reduced Engine Power / Service StabiliTrak from Throttle Body Failure
records.description: Impalas frequently throw a cluster of warnings at once — 'Engine Power Reduced,' 'Service StabiliTrak,' and 'Service Traction Control' — that are usually one underlying drive-by-wire fault rather than three separate failures. The most common root cause is the electronic throttle body actuator (or the dual throttle-position sensors inside it) going out of range; the accelerator pedal position sensors can also disagree. Because the ECM cross-checks these dual sensors, any disagreement forces the car into limp-home mode with drastically reduced power. Carbon buildup on the throttle plate aggravates it, especially in cold weather.
records.solution: Scan for throttle/pedal DTCs before replacing parts. Start by cleaning the throttle body (a frequent cause, cheap fix). If codes/symptoms persist, replace the electronic throttle body assembly (ACDelco 12670981 fits the 2012-2013 3.6L; verify the correct unit for your engine/year). Some 3.6L applications require a relearn/idle relearn after replacement. If the pedal sensors are at fault, replace the accelerator pedal position sensor assembly.
symptoms: 'Engine Power Reduced' message with limp-home mode
'Service StabiliTrak' and 'Service Traction Control' lights together
Sudden loss of acceleration
Rough or surging idle, worse in cold weather
Intermittent recovery after key cycle

records.title: Water Pump and Coolant Crossover Pipe Gasket Leaks (3.5L/3.9L)
records.description: The 3.5L and 3.9L 'high value' V6s develop two common coolant leaks. First, the water pump leaks from its weep hole as the internal seal wears — often visible as coolant sprayed across the serpentine belt and accessories. Second, the cast-aluminum coolant crossover pipe on the right side of the engine (which links the front and rear cylinder heads) uses a gasket at each end that hardens and leaks over time, showing up as coolant near the back of the engine or the head/belt area. Either can cause gradual coolant loss and overheating if ignored.
records.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system to pinpoint the source. A weep-hole drip or coolant flung by the belt means the water pump — replace it (and the belt if soaked). Coolant at the rear/right of the engine points to the crossover pipe gaskets — replace both crossover gaskets. Refill with the correct Dex-Cool and bleed the system. Do not keep driving with a suspected bad water pump; overheating these aluminum engines risks head-gasket damage.
symptoms: Coolant drip from water pump weep hole
Coolant sprayed across belt/accessories
Sweet smell and low coolant level
Coolant residue at rear/right of engine
Rising temperature gauge / overheating

records.title: Power Window Regulator and Motor Failure
records.description: The power window regulators in the 2006-2020 Impala fail frequently, causing windows to fall into the door, move slowly, or stop working entirely. The cable-style regulator uses thin steel cables that fray and break, or the motor gears strip. The driver window is the most commonly affected due to highest usage. In cold weather, ice can bind the window in the channel and burn out the motor when the switch is pressed. Some owners report windows falling into the door with a loud clunk.
records.solution: Replace the window regulator assembly ($60-$150 for parts) — always replace the regulator and motor as a unit since the motor is often damaged by a failed regulator. Labor is 1-2 hours per window ($100-$250). The door panel must be removed for access. Buy a quality aftermarket regulator (Dorman is widely available) or OEM ACDelco. In cold weather, never force a frozen window — use the defroster to warm the door seal before attempting to operate the window.
symptoms: Window falls into the door suddenly
Window moves slowly or stops partway
Grinding or clicking noise when operating window
Window switch clicks but window does not move
Window operates intermittently

citations.title: YouTube - How to Replace Power Window Regulator on Chevrolet Impala (ChrisFix)

communityRecommendations.content: Replace the regulator and motor as a complete assembly. The motor is often damaged by a failed regulator, and replacing just the regulator with a worn motor means you will be doing the job again soon.

records.title: Electric Power Steering Assist Motor Failure
records.description: The 2014-2020 Impala uses an electric power steering system with a motor mounted on the steering column. GM issued a recall for some model years.
records.solution: Replace the electric power steering motor/column assembly. Remanufactured units available from Cardone. Recall coverage may apply - check with dealer.
